content: Calendula officinalis, commonly known as Pot Marigold or English Marigold, is a plant belonging to the Calendula genus. Historically, it has been utilized in ancient Greek, Roman, Arabic, and Indian cultures for its medicinal properties and as a natural dye for textiles, foods, and cosmetics. The leaves and petals of Pot Marigold are edible. The petals are often used as a garnish in culinary dishes and can serve as a substitute for saffron. While the leaves may have a sweet taste, they are more commonly bitter and are sometimes incorporated into salads. In homeopathic medicine, Calendula is frequently used in gel form to promote the healing of minor burns, scrapes, and skin irritations. Medical Uses The flowers of Calendula, when harvested between June and September, are at their most potent. Hot Calendula tea is known to alleviate ulcers, while cool Calendula tea can be used as a gargle to soothe inflamed tonsils or canker sores. To prepare the tea, one can either: Pour 10 ounces of boiling water over 2/3 cup of dried Calendula flowers and allow it to steep for 15 minutes, or Add 5–10 drops of Calendula tincture to a cup of hot water. Calendula ointment is applied to scabs, eczema, and psoriasis. To make the ointment: 1. Melt 1/2 cup of petroleum jelly over low heat using a double boiler. 2. Add a handful of dried Calendula flowers. 3. Heat the mixture on low for one hour. 4. Strain out the herbs and pour the mixture into a glass jar for storage. Calendula tincture or spray can be applied to rashes, cuts, scrapes, or acne using a cotton ball. Sprays are particularly effective for sunburns, vaginitis, and pinworm infestations. To dry the flowers for later use, place them on a mesh surface in direct sunlight for 1–2 weeks, then store them in an airtight container. Pharmacology Calendula is widely used for the treatment of skin disorders, pain relief, and as a bactericide, antiseptic, and anti-inflammatory agent. The petals and pollen of the plant contain triterpenoid esters, which have anti-inflammatory properties, as well as carotenoids such as flavoxanthin and auroxanthin, which act as antioxidants and are responsible for the plant's yellow-orange coloration. The leaves and stems are rich in other carotenoids, primarily lutein (80%), zeaxanthin (5%), and beta-carotene. Plant extracts from Calendula are also extensively used in the cosmetics industry, likely due to the presence of compounds such as saponins, resins, and essential oils. Preliminary studies have even suggested that organic extracts of Calendula may inhibit HIV-1.
